content.text:
Upstream OrcaSlicer puts exactly one credential in the operating system's secret store: the refresh token for signing in to Orca Cloud, OrcaSlicer's own cloud account service. Nothing else goes there. Printer passwords, printer API keys and Bambu cloud credentials are all stored somewhere else.

I checked this in this repo's copy of the upstream code, not on upstream's current `main` branch. The file was written by SoftFever, the upstream maintainer, in January 2026, so it is upstream code. Upstream may have changed it since this fork branched.

**What goes in the secret store** ([OrcaCloudServiceAgent.cpp:80](src/slic3r/Utils/OrcaCloudServiceAgent.cpp:80))
- It uses `wxSecretStore`, which is Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows and libsecret on Linux.
- Service name: `OrcaSlicer/Auth`. Username: `orca_refresh_token`.
- The value is either a bare refresh token or a JSON object with `refresh_token`, `user_id`, `username` and `nickname` ([parse_stored_secret, line 569](src/slic3r/Utils/OrcaCloudServiceAgent.cpp:569)). Only the refresh token is a secret; the other fields let the app restore a signed-in session without a network call.
- The short-lived access token is kept in memory only. It is never saved.
- If several OrcaSlicer windows are open, the keychain copy is the one they trust. Refreshes are serialized with a lock shared between processes, so two windows don't both use the same refresh token.

**Alternative: an encrypted file**
- Preferences has a setting "Store authentication tokens in an encrypted file instead of the system keychain" (`use_encrypted_token_file` in AppConfig).
- With it on, the same data goes to `orca_refresh_token.sec` in the config folder instead. The file is AES-256-GCM encrypted and signed with an HMAC.
- Signing out deletes both the keychain entry and the file.

**Credentials that are not in the secret store**
- **Printer connection settings** (`printhost_apikey`, `printhost_user`, `printhost_password` for OctoPrint, Moonraker and similar): saved as plain text in the physical printer's `.ini` preset.
- **Bambu cloud login**: handled inside Bambu's closed-source network plugin, which stores its own data. I didn't find any secret-store calls for it in the OrcaSlicer source.

In this fork, [AgentConfiguration.cpp](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentConfiguration.cpp) also uses `wxSecretStore` for the Agent's API key. That code is fork-only and doesn't exist upstream.

content.text:
The easiest way to test this is with an official OrcaSlicer release rather than this repo's build. Sign in to Orca Cloud, then check macOS Keychain for an entry named `OrcaSlicer/Auth`. This fork can't start that sign-in at all: it replaces Orca's Home page (which has the sign-in button) with its own, and the fork's page never sends the sign-in command. The only other place Orca Cloud appears is File → Sync Presets, and that menu item is disabled until you're signed in.

The automated tests don't cover storage either. [slic3rutils_tests_main.cpp](tests/slic3rutils/slic3rutils_tests_main.cpp) only tests how the display name is read from a session.

**Manual test with an OrcaSlicer release on macOS**

1. Install an OrcaSlicer release that includes Orca Cloud sign-in. I haven't checked which release number added it.
2. Before signing in, confirm there's no entry. I ran this and got "could not be found":
   ```bash
   security find-generic-password -s "OrcaSlicer/Auth"
   ```
   This prints only the entry's metadata. Adding `-w` would print the refresh token itself, so don't paste that output anywhere.
3. On the Home page, click the Orca Cloud log-in button and finish signing in in the browser. If Stealth Mode is on, the app asks you to turn it off first.
4. Run the `security` command again. You should now see an entry, which you can also find by searching "OrcaSlicer" in the Keychain Access app. I expect the service field to be `OrcaSlicer/Auth` and the account field to be `orca_refresh_token`. I haven't checked how wxWidgets maps these to Keychain fields, because its source isn't in this repo. The app looks the entry up by service name only.
5. Quit and reopen the app. You should still be signed in, because the session is read back from Keychain. Try it with Wi-Fi off too, since a recent upstream change lets you work offline while signed in.
6. Sign out from the Home page. The entry should be gone.

**Encrypted-file mode**

1. In Preferences, turn on "Store authentication tokens in an encrypted file instead of the system keychain", then restart.
2. Sign in. Check that `~/Library/Application Support/OrcaSlicer/orca_refresh_token.sec` now exists and holds unreadable encrypted text starting with `v2:`.
3. Restart. You should still be signed in.
4. Sign out. The file should be deleted. Signing out also deletes any Keychain entry.

**To test it in a JusPrin build instead**

You'd need a temporary way to send `homepage_orca_login_or_register` to the app, such as a debug menu item that calls `wxGetApp().request_login(true, ORCA_CLOUD_PROVIDER)`. Everything after sign-in would work the same, except that the settings and the `.sec` file live in `~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/`. The Keychain service name stays `OrcaSlicer/Auth`, because it's a fixed string in the code and isn't renamed with the app. I can add that temporary hook if you want.
When I tried to create an account in OrcaSizer, I got this page. It appears that it's bamboo, not OrcaCloud.

You're right: that page is Bambu's sign-in, not Orca Cloud. The OrcaSlicer on this Mac is version 2.3.1, which has no Orca Cloud at all, so its "login / register" button can only sign you in to Bambu's cloud. "Bambu Handy" is Bambu's phone app, and Bambu's Google sign-in uses that name. You can click **Cancel**; nothing has been stored yet.

**What I checked**
- The installed app at `/Applications/OrcaSlicer.app` reports version 2.3.1, and its program file has none of the Orca Cloud strings (`OrcaSlicer/Auth`, `orca_refresh_token`, `orcaslicer-login`).
- 2.3.1 was tagged in October 2025. The Orca Cloud code was first added in January 2026.
- 2.3.2 (March 2026) includes the Orca Cloud code, but its server addresses are placeholders (`https://xxx.orcaslicer.com`), so sign-in doesn't work there either.
- 2.4.2 (July 2026, the latest release) has real server addresses. Its Home page has separate sign-in areas for Orca and for Bambu. The top "login / register" button signs in to Orca Cloud, and a second "login" button further down signs in to Bambu.

**To run the test**
1. Quit the running OrcaSlicer 2.3.1.
2. Install OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 from https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer/releases/tag/v2.4.2.
3. Follow the Keychain steps from my previous message, using the top "login / register" button in the Orca section of the Home page. The sign-in page should be an OrcaSlicer page, not a Google screen mentioning Bambu Handy.

2.4.2 will probably use the same settings folder, `~/Library/Application Support/OrcaSlicer`, as 2.3.1. It may update your 2.3.1 settings, so back up that folder first if you want to keep them.

The dialog appears because JusPrin still contains OrcaSlicer's Orca Cloud sign-in code, and that code reads the Keychain entry OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 created when you signed in today. macOS lets an app read an entry silently only if the app is signed in a way the entry already trusts. OrcaSlicer created the entry, so it's trusted. JusPrin is a different app, so macOS asks you first.

This probably started today: before you signed in to OrcaSlicer 2.4.2, there was no `OrcaSlicer/Auth` entry for JusPrin to find.

**Where the read happens**

When the Orca Cloud agent starts, `OrcaCloudServiceAgent::start()` calls `load_user_secret()` to restore the previous sign-in ([OrcaCloudServiceAgent.cpp:603](src/slic3r/Utils/OrcaCloudServiceAgent.cpp:603)). That looks up the fixed service name `OrcaSlicer/Auth`. The fork never renamed it, so JusPrin reads the same entry as OrcaSlicer.

**Why the two apps get different treatment**

| | OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 | Your JusPrin build |
|---|---|---|
| Bundle ID | `com.orcaslicer.OrcaSlicer` | `io.jusprin.JusPrin` |
| Signature | Developer ID, team `XQK7C38HH5` | ad-hoc, meaning signed locally with no developer identity |
| How macOS identifies it | bundle ID plus team ID, which stay the same across releases | a hash of this exact build: `cdhash 4c415b9f…` |

**Why it comes back every launch**

- **Clicking "Allow"** grants access once, so the next launch asks again.
- **Clicking "Always Allow"** trusts this exact build by its hash. An ad-hoc build gets a new hash every time you rebuild, so after a rebuild the prompt returns.

I haven't confirmed which of these you're hitting. I tried to read which apps the entry trusts, but `security dump-keychain` hung for over two minutes, so I stopped it before it could trigger more prompts.

**What to do now**

- **Deny** is safe. JusPrin just won't restore an Orca Cloud sign-in, which it has no button for anyway, and OrcaSlicer keeps working.
- **Signing out of Orca Cloud in OrcaSlicer** deletes the entry, and the prompt goes away. This also finishes your sign-out test.
- **Don't enter your password or click Always Allow** just to silence it. That would give JusPrin your Orca Cloud refresh token, and the app would then refresh it. Orca Cloud replaces the refresh token each time it's used, so JusPrin could invalidate the token OrcaSlicer has saved and sign OrcaSlicer out.

**The real fix belongs in the fork**

JusPrin shouldn't read OrcaSlicer's Orca Cloud credentials at all. There are two options:
1. Rename the Keychain service to something JusPrin-specific. That's a one-line change to a file owned by upstream OrcaSlicer.
2. Don't start the Orca Cloud agent in JusPrin, since the fork has no Orca Cloud sign-in button.

Option 2 is the cleaner product fix, but it touches more upstream code. I haven't reproduced this in a JusPrin build yet. Per your bug-fix rule, I'd do that first. Want me to?

You're right, option 1 is a clean fix. I was wrong to rank option 2 above it. I hadn't checked what the Orca Cloud agent does in JusPrin without a stored token, and the answer is almost nothing, so turning it off wouldn't gain much.

**What the agent does without a token**
- At launch, `OrcaCloudServiceAgent::start()` generates a random code for a future sign-in (no network) and looks up the stored token. The lookup is the only part that reaches the Keychain, and the only part that causes the dialog.
- The health check, `connect_server()`, doesn't run on a plain launch. It runs when the user signs in ([GUI_App.cpp:5193](src/slic3r/GUI/GUI_App.cpp:5193)) or after networking restarts ([GUI_App.cpp:1798](src/slic3r/GUI/GUI_App.cpp:1798)).
- With a JusPrin-specific Keychain name, the lookup finds nothing. macOS only asks permission when an entry exists, so nothing would be left for option 2 to fix.

**Why option 1 is clean**
- **It fits the fork's pattern.** Everything else JusPrin stores is already separated from OrcaSlicer's by the app key (`SLIC3R_APP_KEY`, which is `JusPrin2` here). That includes the settings folder (`JusPrin2/`), the settings file (`JusPrin2.conf`), and the encrypted token file. The Keychain entry is the one exception, because its name is a fixed string.
- **It needs no JusPrin branding in upstream code.** Change the service name to `SLIC3R_APP_KEY "/Auth"`. Upstream's key is `OrcaSlicer`, so it still gets `OrcaSlicer/Auth`, and JusPrin gets `JusPrin2/Auth`. That makes it a behavior-neutral change upstream could accept, which suits `fork-stewardship.md`'s rules for editing upstream files.
- **Rebase risk is minimal.** The two lines defining the Keychain names haven't changed since the file was created in January 2026.
- **It fixes the refresh-token problem on every platform.** On Windows and Linux there's no dialog, so JusPrin silently shares OrcaSlicer's token today. If JusPrin ever refreshed that token, OrcaSlicer's saved copy would stop working. Renaming separates them.
- **Nobody loses a sign-in.** JusPrin has no Orca Cloud sign-in button, so no JusPrin user has a token under the old name.

Option 2 is a separate product question: whether JusPrin should include Orca Cloud at all. That affects things like the File → Sync Presets menu, and it's not needed to fix this dialog.

Following your bug-fix rule, I'd first reproduce the dialog with a JusPrin build. Then I'd make the one-line change, rebuild, and confirm JusPrin launches without the dialog while OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 stays signed in. Should I go ahead?

I've fixed the Orca Cloud part of the dialog. JusPrin now keeps its Orca Cloud sign-in in its own Keychain entry, `JusPrin2/Auth`, and no longer touches OrcaSlicer's `OrcaSlicer/Auth` entry. A rebuilt JusPrin will still show a second, separate Keychain dialog after each rebuild, for the Agent's API key. That one is JusPrin's own code, and this change doesn't fix it. Nothing is committed.

**The change** ([OrcaCloudServiceAgent.cpp:80](src/slic3r/Utils/OrcaCloudServiceAgent.cpp:80))
```diff
-constexpr const char* SECRET_STORE_SERVICE = "OrcaSlicer/Auth";
+// Keyed by app so forks built from this source don't read OrcaSlicer's token ("OrcaSlicer/Auth" upstream).
+constexpr const char* SECRET_STORE_SERVICE = SLIC3R_APP_KEY "/Auth";
```
The name now comes from the app key: upstream still gets `OrcaSlicer/Auth`, and JusPrin gets `JusPrin2/Auth`.

**Before the fix** (build from HEAD `0c35f92d97`, while you were signed in to OrcaSlicer 2.4.2)
- JusPrin stopped at startup, and macOS's dialog process started.
- The sample of the main thread showed it waiting in `OrcaCloudServiceAgent::start()` → `load_user_secret()` → `SecKeychainFindGenericPassword`.

**After the fix** (rebuilt binary, 09:14)
- The binary contains `JusPrin2/Auth` and no longer contains `OrcaSlicer/Auth`.
- With the Agent turned off in the scratch settings, JusPrin started normally: no new dialog process, main thread in the normal event loop.
- The only Keychain call was a brief lookup for `JusPrin2/Auth` (explained below). That entry doesn't exist, so macOS had nothing to ask.
- `OrcaSlicer/Auth` still exists, unchanged since your sign-in at 16:12:33 UTC.

**The second dialog, not fixed by this change**
- A rebuilt JusPrin also asks for `JusPrin Agent OpenAI`, from [AgentConfiguration.cpp:47](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentConfiguration.cpp:47).
- macOS trusts a local build by a hash of its exact binary, and each rebuild changes that hash, so the dialog returns after every rebuild.
- In my second test run, that dialog blocked startup before the Orca Cloud code ran. That's why I turned the Agent off in the scratch settings copy for the final run. Your real settings are unchanged.
- Fixing this means signing builds with a stable identity rather than ad-hoc. That's a separate decision.

**A worse problem the fix also removes (inference, not verified)**
- Every 2 seconds, a JusPrin that isn't signed in to Orca Cloud runs a sign-in status check. That check calls `clear_user_secret()`, which deletes the Keychain entry.
- Before the fix, it targeted `OrcaSlicer/Auth`. If you ever clicked Allow on the dialog, JusPrin could have deleted OrcaSlicer's saved sign-in, signing you out of OrcaSlicer.
- That could explain why the entry was gone earlier, when I assumed you had signed out. OrcaSlicer's logs can't settle it, because they don't record sign-ins or sign-outs at the default log level. Did you actually sign out in OrcaSlicer?

**Rebase record** (required by `fork-stewardship.md` for changes to upstream files)
1. **Rebase check:** from fork base `3ffb9585d2`, a temporary commit with this change onto `upstream/main` `70247ad298` (fetched today) merges with no conflicts. The merged file has the new line at 94–95. Upstream still defines `SLIC3R_APP_KEY "OrcaSlicer"`, and `Http.hpp` still includes the header that provides it.
2. **Upstream lines changed:** one line rewritten, none deleted. Only the name's value changed. It couldn't be a pure addition because the name is a single constant.
3. **What the fork now owns:** a neutral naming change. It doesn't change upstream's behavior and could be sent upstream as-is.

**Not done**
- No commit.
- No automated test. The name is a constant private to one source file, so there's nothing to call from a test. The before-and-after launches above are the verification.
- Not checked on Windows or Linux. Those builds use the same line, so they would also switch to `JusPrin2/Auth`.

I committed the fix as `81fe1b2c8c` ("Key the Orca Cloud Keychain entry by app") on `jusprin-newui`. It isn't pushed.

The best check for a production JusPrin build is to sign a local build with the production certificate and test it on this Mac. This repo's CI can't produce a signed JusPrin Mac build right now (details below), but this Mac has the certificate: "Developer ID Application: TSD Technology, LLC (VR5RXL44RC)". Two different dialogs matter, and each needs its own check.

**1. The `OrcaSlicer/Auth` dialog (the one just fixed)**

Signing doesn't change whether this dialog appears. Even a production-signed JusPrin is a different app from OrcaSlicer, so before the fix it would have prompted too. After the fix, JusPrin never looks up `OrcaSlicer/Auth` at all. To confirm on the signed build:
- Check the app binary contains `JusPrin2/Auth` and doesn't contain `OrcaSlicer/Auth`.
- With OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 signed in, launch the signed JusPrin. There should be no dialog, and `OrcaSlicer/Auth` should still exist afterwards. Then leave JusPrin open for a few minutes, because its sign-in status check runs every 2 seconds.

**2. The `JusPrin Agent OpenAI` dialog (still appears after every local rebuild)**

This comes from how macOS decides which app may read a Keychain entry:
- For a Developer ID-signed app, macOS should trust "bundle ID `io.jusprin.JusPrin` signed by team VR5RXL44RC". Every production update matches that, so updates shouldn't prompt.
- For a local unsigned (ad-hoc) build, macOS trusts only that exact binary, which is why each rebuild prompts.
- I'm inferring the first point from what we saw: OrcaSlicer's signed app is identified by bundle ID and team, our local build only by a binary hash. It hasn't been tested with JusPrin.
- The signing entitlements (`scripts/disable_validation.entitlements`) only turn off library validation and declare no Keychain groups, so nothing there should change this.

The test:
1. Build, sign with Developer ID using the same `codesign` flags as `build_orca.yml`, and launch.
2. Save a test key through Agent setup, so the Keychain entry is created by the signed build.
3. Make a trivial change, rebuild, and sign again. The binary is now different but has the same identity, like a production update.
4. Launch it. There should be no dialog.

One expected exception: your existing `JusPrin Agent OpenAI` entry was created by a local unsigned build. The first signed build will prompt for it once. After Always Allow, later signed builds shouldn't prompt. New users won't see this, since their first entry is created by a signed build.

Notarization shouldn't affect either dialog, because it only matters when you open a downloaded app. The fully realistic check is to install a notarized DMG and repeat both tests.

**Gap in CI**

The "Sign app and notary" step in `build_orca.yml` now runs only when `github.repository == 'OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer'`. That came from upstream. JusPrin v1.4.0's workflow signed on `main` and `release/*` branches instead. So CI in `TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin` always builds an unsigned, un-notarized DMG, and a production build from this branch would behave like the local builds: prompting after every update. Fixing that means choosing branches and setting signing secrets for this repository, which is your decision.

Should I run the signed-build test? It needs your login password once, when macOS asks whether `codesign` may use the TSD certificate; you'd type it in the macOS dialog, not in this chat. It also needs one real click on Always Allow for the existing Agent entry (the exception above).
